items.notes: Subject: literature. 65 words (models' median 57). Section 6: rule R1; 18 run words after the blank; cue outside the 6-word window (the head each one sits 20 words before the blank); plural attractors variations, imitations, telegrams, letters (the last two right before the blank), an intervener verb of the other number (range) and a plural cue after the blank (together they demonstrate). Options vary on number and finiteness: two plural forms and the nonfinite recounting. Blind solve: only recounts; recount and have recounted are plural, recounting leaves each one without a verb.
items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: each one of + plural noun, with a plural-verb relative clause between
items.passage: French writer Raymond Queneau’s 1947 book Exercises in Style retells a trivial anecdote, a quarrel between passengers on a crowded Paris bus, in 99 versions. Each one of the book’s variations, which range from the ode and the sonnet to imitations of telegrams and official letters, ______ the incident in a distinctive register, and together they demonstrate how thoroughly style can transform identical narrative material.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the first clause is “each one,” which is singular; “of the book’s variations” and the clause “which range ... letters” only describe it, and “they” in the second clause refers to all the variations together. The blank must supply the finite verb for “each one,” and “recounts” is the only option that is both finite and singular.

B.why_wrong: The plural “recount” fits “official letters” right before the blank and matches the plural “range” and “they demonstrate” around it, but the subject is the singular “each one.”

C.why_wrong: The plural “have recounted” does not agree with the singular subject “each one.”

D.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed
D.why_wrong: The participle “recounting” is not plural, but it leaves “each one of the book’s variations” without a finite verb, so everything before “and together” is a fragment.

plural attractors between head and blank: variations, imitations, telegrams, letters (singular head behind plurals)
options vary on number and finiteness: recounting is not plural but leaves the clause without a verb

band7.why: The section-5 R1_quant_compound setting of 0fe5ce68: singular head each one of + plural noun, a relative clause with its own plural verb (range) and five plural attractors, the last two touching the blank, so the plural sounds right twice; head 24 words before the blank, 15 run words after it. items.notes: Subject: ornithology. 62 words (models' median 38). Section 6: R2_interrupter with the comma-only key (1a61e2ae, d222f7d9); the participle implanted is in the passage; 11 words from the blank to the main verb flew; garden-path check: cut before flew, E7 was, E7, was and E7 had been each give a complete, sensible passive clause; 44 run words after the blank. With the key the sentence has one finite main verb (flew); with each distractor two, joined only by a comma, and C also puts a lone comma between subject and verb. No and follows flew, so no finite option can start a series of predicates (an earlier draft with left ..., and landed let E7 was read as was implanted, left, and landed). Distance given as more than 11,000 kilometers because sources range from 11,500 to 11,680 (7,200 miles). Blind solve: only E7,.
items.subtype: Comma-only key: past-participle supplement (implanted ...) between the subject and its delayed main verb, 11 words
items.passage: Some bar-tailed godwits breed in Alaska and overwinter in New Zealand and Australia. A female godwit designated ______ implanted with a satellite transmitter in New Zealand in February 2007, flew nonstop from Alaska’s Yukon-Kuskokwim Delta to New Zealand between August 29 and September 7, 2007, covering more than 11,000 kilometers in the longest uninterrupted migratory flight then documented for any bird.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the second sentence is “a female godwit designated E7,” and its finite main verb is “flew.” The words “implanted with ... February 2007” form a supplementary participial phrase describing E7; the comma after “E7” pairs with the comma after “2007” to set it off. A finite verb in the blank (“was,” “had been”) would give the sentence a second main verb with no conjunction.

A.recipe: finite where a nonfinite is needed
A.why_wrong: “A female godwit designated E7 was implanted ... in February 2007” reads as a complete clause, but then “flew” has no subject of its own: two main verbs are joined only by a comma, with no conjunction.

C.recipe: finite where a nonfinite is needed; punctuation also wrong
C.why_wrong: The comma pairs with the one after “2007,” so the phrase looks set off, but “was implanted” is a finite verb, a single comma cannot separate a subject from its verb, and the sentence again has two main verbs.

D.recipe: finite where a nonfinite is needed
D.why_wrong: “Had been implanted” suits an event earlier than the August flight, but it is a finite verb, so it competes with the main verb “flew,” and the two predicates are joined only by a comma.

band7_moves: R2_interrupter, comma-only key: the participle implanted is in the passage and the comma sits in the options, as in 1a61e2ae and d222f7d9

band7.why: R2_interrupter, the band-7-only template: a restrictive participial phrase with no commas (as in 4 of 9 models) and the main verb confirmed 9 words after the blank; every finite option makes Ornithologists ... in New Zealand a complete, sensible clause, so the error only shows at confirmed. One -ing against three finite forms of the same verb, as in 505054e3 and c9a677e9.

hardened.what: Rebuilt on the comma-only key of 1a61e2ae and d222f7d9: the participle implanted sits in the passage and the comma is folded into the options (E7 was, E7, / E7, was, E7 had been), so finiteness and punctuation are decided together. Each finite option turns the subject and the next 11 words into a complete, natural passive clause; the error shows only at flew, 11 words after the blank. The main predicate is one verb with no and after it, so a finite option cannot be read as the first of a series (was implanted ..., flew ...).
tempting: A: A female godwit designated E7 was implanted with a satellite transmitter in New Zealand in February 2007 is a complete, natural clause, while the bare E7, looks unfinished; it fails only at flew, 11 words on
C: its comma pairs with the comma after 2007, so the phrase looks properly set off; the verb is still finite and the comma splits subject from verb
D: the past perfect suits an event earlier than the August flight, so a tense check approves it; it is still a second main verb

items.notes: Subject: zoology (biomaterials). 36 words (models' median 32.5). Section 6: R3 key subject is a property (the dragline silk of ...), not the obvious noun (the spider) that ends the first sentence; options 17 to 19 words, all grammatical and keeping every fact; key not the longest. Distractors after hardening: W possessive naming the wrong part (Darwin’s bark spider’s webs), W (the spider, passive with the study as an interrupter), W noun + of + spider (a 2010 study of Darwin’s bark spider). Blind solve: only C, because that of any other spider means the silk of any other spider. Toughness figure from Agnarsson et al. 2010 (more than twice any previously described silk); radial threads are where the paper took its dragline samples.
items.subtype: Compared with that of ...: the right subject is a property (the silk), not the animal
items.passage: Darwin’s bark spider, endemic to Madagascar, suspends enormous orb webs above rivers and lakes, anchoring them to either bank with threads extending up to 25 meters. Compared with that of any other spider previously examined, ______
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: Darwin’s bark spider’s webs have radial threads of dragline silk more than twice as tough, a 2010 study found.
Darwin’s bark spider was found, in a 2010 study, to produce dragline silk more than twice as tough.
the dragline silk of Darwin’s bark spider is more than twice as tough, a 2010 study found.
a 2010 study of Darwin’s bark spider found its dragline silk to be more than twice as tough.
items.explanation: The opening phrase compares something with “that of any other spider,” and what is more than twice as tough is silk, so “that” stands for the dragline silk of other spiders and the noun right after the phrase must be Darwin’s bark spider’s silk. Choice C places “the dragline silk of Darwin’s bark spider” immediately after the modifier. The webs (A), the spider (B) and a study (D) are not what is compared with other spiders’ silk.

A.recipe: W: wrong noun as subject (a possessive naming the wrong part, the webs)
A.why_wrong: Placing “Darwin’s bark spider’s webs” right after the phrase illogically compares the webs with other spiders’ silk; the singular “that” cannot stand for the plural “webs” either.

B.recipe: W: wrong noun as subject (the spider, with the study as an interrupter)
B.why_wrong: Placing “Darwin’s bark spider” right after the phrase illogically compares the spider itself with other spiders’ silk; the interrupting “was found, in a 2010 study,” does not change the subject.

D.recipe: W: wrong noun as subject (the study, built as noun + of + spider)
D.why_wrong: Placing “a 2010 study of Darwin’s bark spider” right after the phrase illogically compares a study with other spiders’ silk, even though it has the same “of” + spider shape as “that of any other spider.”

band7_moves: Compared with that of ... opener, so the right subject is a property (the silk), not the obvious noun (the spider)
two distractors look like property subjects: a possessive naming the wrong part (the webs) and a noun + of + spider phrase (a 2010 study of Darwin’s bark spider)
the obvious noun ends the first sentence and opens the third distractor (B), as silica glass does in 2dd1b8bf
options of 17 to 19 words, all grammatical sentences, keeping every fact; key not the longest option

sources.what: Agnarsson, Kuntner and Blackledge 2010, PLoS ONE: Darwin's bark spider silk toughness averages 350 MJ/m3, more than twice tougher than any previously described silk; webs suspended above streams, rivers and lakes with anchor threads up to 25 m; dragline silk samples were taken from the radial threads of the orb web
Madagascar spider silk ten times tougher than Kevlar; species from Madagascar

fixes: hardened: B (a 2010 study found that ...) and D (there is ... , no study) died on sight; B now opens with the spider in a passive frame with the study as an interrupter (8b017d4e style), D keeps the expletive but carries every fact, so two distractors start with the obvious noun as in 2dd1b8bf and fced396a

hardened after gate2 (Haiku p(key) 0.92): A now a possessive naming the wrong part (Darwin’s bark spider’s webs, radial threads sourced to the PMC methods), D now a 2010 study of Darwin’s bark spider in place of the expletive

band7.why: After hardening: the Compared with that of opener forces a property subject (the silk of the spider), the 3-of-5 band-7 R3 setting; two distractors open with the spider, the noun the opener seems to describe, one of them a natural passive with the study inside it. Before the fix two of the three distractors (the study, there) were killed at a glance, which read as band 6.

hardened.what: The spider-first active option (A) became a possessive naming the wrong part (Darwin’s bark spider’s webs), the shape of the key in 2dd1b8bf, and the expletive (D) became a 2010 study of Darwin’s bark spider, a noun + of + spider phrase that mirrors that of any other spider. Two distractors now look like property subjects; only the silk is what that stands for.
tempting: A: a possessive subject like the key of 2dd1b8bf, so a student who knows that of calls for a property picks it; but the webs are not what is compared, and plural webs cannot match singular that
B: the spider, the noun that ends the first sentence and seems to be what the opener describes, inside a natural passive with the study tucked in
D: a 2010 study of Darwin’s bark spider copies the shape of that of any other spider and its clause keeps every fact; the study is not what is compared

items.notes: Subject: linguistics and music. 57 words (models' median 53). Section 6: plural head (pitches) behind four singular nouns (drummer, membrane, gángan, drum) and an intervener verb of the other number (generates); head 22 words before the blank, so the cue is outside the window; 12 run words after the blank. Options vary on number and finiteness: two singular forms and the nonfinite mirroring. Blind solve: only mirror; mirrors matches the nearest nouns, mirroring leaves pitches without a verb. The claim stays within Akinbo's abstract (drummers tighten and loosen the membrane to produce the three tones and can represent syllables and tones).
items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: plural head behind a relative clause with a singular verb and singular nouns
items.passage: Yorùbá is a tonal language: a syllable’s relative pitch (high, mid, or low) can distinguish otherwise identical words. According to linguist Samuel Akinbo, the fluctuating pitches that a drummer generates by alternately tightening and loosening the membrane of a gángan, an hourglass-shaped talking drum, ______ these three tones precisely enough to represent individual Yorùbá syllables and words.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the main clause is the plural noun “pitches”; everything from “that a drummer generates” to “talking drum” describes those pitches. The blank must supply that subject’s finite verb, and “mirror” is the only option that is both finite and plural.

A.why_wrong: The singular “mirrors” agrees with the nearby singular nouns (“drum,” “gángan,” “drummer”), not with the plural subject “pitches.”

B.why_wrong: The singular “has mirrored” does not agree with the plural subject “pitches.”

C.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed
C.why_wrong: “Mirroring” reads well after “talking drum,” as if it described the drum or the drumming, and it carries no singular ending, but it leaves “the fluctuating pitches” with no finite verb, so the sentence has no main clause.
